title: cluster-iptables-rewrite-dns-latency-scratchpad
content:
Summary:

Short: On 2024-11-03 morning deploy window we observed a cluster-wide spike in pod DNS resolution latency and intermittent service-to-service failures. Root cause appears to be repeated iptables policy rewrites from kube-proxy during a kube-proxy restart loop on a subset of nodes, which overwhelmed conntrack and caused NAT/forward path stalls.

Impact:
- ~12% of requests to internal services returned 502/504 for 42 minutes.
- DNS latency (coredns) p50 increased from ~10ms to ~120ms; p95 hit ~1.8s.
- Sidecar-heavy deployments (prometheus exporters, proxy-init) saw higher degradation.
- Billing/ingress paths degraded resulting in increased latency observed by end-to-end SLO monitors.

Detection timeline (UTC):
- 07:02: Prometheus alert: internal-http-error-rate > threshold for route /api/*
- 07:05: Pager duty to oncall (Avery).
- 07:07: Slack thread #sre-ops started; initial triage begun.
- 07:10: Observed coredns latency spike on prometheus panels.
- 07:15: Noted large rate of kube-proxy restarts on nodes in us-west-2a (k8s nodes labeled gpu-pool-2).
- 07:20: TCP conntrack table on affected nodes nearing 96% usage (node-exporter conntrack_count).
- 07:30: Applied temporary iptables conntrack cleanup and scaled kube-proxy replicas to 0/2 on a small test subset for repro.
- 07:44: Stabilization observed after incremental conntrack pruning and kube-proxy pinning; 502/504s fell to baseline.

Initial triage notes and commands run (notes-to-self style):
- Checked kube-proxy status: kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l k8s-app=kube-proxy -o wide
- Notice: CrashLoopBackOff on 3/120 nodes in us-west-2a. Logs: kubectl -n kube-system logs kube-proxy-xyz --previous
  - repeated errors: "failed to build iptables rules: file too big" and "OOM when writing kernel table"
- conntrack metrics: ssh node -> sudo conntrack -L | wc -l (we saw spikes 1.1M -> 3.8M entries)
- Kernel dmesg on affected nodes: OOM killer invoked on kube-proxy? (evidence: memory pressure + ip_tables module warnings)
- Verified iptables-save output was large and contained many ephemeral CIDR blocks from service endpoints (flapping endpoints caused churn).

Mitigations applied (ordered):
1) Rolling cordon of affected nodes, moved pods to healthy nodes in other AZs (kubectl cordon; drain with --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data).
2) On one repro node: sudo conntrack -F (flush) after coordination with team and routing teams; we rate-limited flushes to avoid tearing in-flight connections.
3) Temporarily scaled DaemonSet kube-proxy to 0 then back to 1 to force a cold recompile of iptables rules, watching conntrack and iptables rule count.
4) Applied conservative kube-proxy flag in cluster-config: --conntrack-max-per-core increased, and --iptables-min-sync-period increased to 10s to reduce churn.

Why this is interesting / unusual:
- Not classic node cpu/memory pressure; kernel-level conntrack exhaustion amplified by kube-proxy restart churn and a burst of pod endpoint churn (abrupt deployment of 400 small short-lived jobs in one namespace around the same time).
- Calico was not directly at fault (we use calico for policy), but the combined effect of ipset updates and kube-proxy iptables rewrites created a heavier-than-usual critical path.

Metrics and graphs we referenced (placeholders for final postmortem):
- PromQL used: sum(rate(kube_proxy_iptables_rules_total[5m])) by (instance)
- Conntrack gauge: node_conntrack_entries / node_conntrack_max (alert fired at >85% for >3m)
- coredns_request_duration_seconds_bucket{le="0.1"} and p95/p99 panels

Root cause hypothesis (working):
- Rapid endpoint churn (CI job burst + a canary) triggered a flurry of ipset and iptables updates from kube-proxy on nodes.
- Kube-proxy attempted frequent rule rewrites; kernel conntrack had been near capacity and rewrites caused transient conntrack table scans/allocs, leading to packet processing stalls for NAT paths (DNS and service mesh traffic).
- Some kube-proxy processes entered restart loops due to memory spikes while computing the ruleset (observed OOM patterns in logs).

Open questions / unknowns:
- Why did endpoint churn spike without obvious orchestrator event? (CI team deployed a large test run; check CI job schedule and autoscaling events).
- Were kernel conntrack sizes set appropriately for our node surfacings? (check /proc/sys/net/netfilter/nf_conntrack_max across older image families).
- Did any node-level sysctl differ in the affected AZ? (compare kubelet/kmod versions and AMI bake dates).

Temporary and permanent follow-ups (action items):
- Immediate (owners):
  - Rina: coordinate with CI to throttle bursty job scheduling in prod-like namespaces. (due: 2024-11-05)
  - Diego: run audit across AMIs for conntrack sysctl settings, collect baseline values. (due: 2024-11-06)
  - Samira: create a short-term auto-remediation for conntrack >75% that alerts and suggests safe conntrack pruning. (due: 2024-11-07)
- Medium term:
  - Evaluate migrating kube-proxy to ipvs mode on GPU pools (pro: fewer rules, con: different failure modes). Owner: eng-serving-runtime. (target Q1 2025)
  - Add targeted alert: kube-proxy rule compile time per node > 5s for 3m. (owner: eng-sre)
  - Increase conntrack_max for legacy AMIs and bake into new AMIs with kernel tuning docs. (owner: platform-engineering)
- Long term:
  - Replace default service endpoint handling for high-churn namespaces with a lightweight dataplane (explore eBPF-based proxies or ipvs + endpoint sharding).

Runbook draft changes (notes for PR):
- New section: "High conntrack utilization and kube-proxy churn" including: detection queries, safe conntrack flush procedure (staged flush, wait 30s between nodes), and kube-proxy restart steps.
- Add troubleshooting checklist for "DNS degraded with normal node CPU": check conntrack entries, kube-proxy restarts, endpoint churn in namespace, recent CI job runs.

Post-incident retrospective notes (meeting prep):
- Bring up why CI run scheduling occurred at the window (invite CI eng, release eng).
- Discuss whether node AMI variance contributed.
- Walk through the mitigation timeline and test the staged conntrack prune procedure on a canary pool.

Raw log excerpts (anonymized):
- "E1103 07:09:41.123 kube-proxy.go:312] failed to write iptables rules: write /proc/sys/net/netfilter/ip_tables: file too big"
- "kernel: nf_conntrack: table full, dropping packet"

Notes to self (informal):
- We should practice the staged conntrack flush in a chaos run (simulate burst of short-lived jobs).
- Consider adding a small per-namespace rate limit for endpoint churn via admission webhook (maybe overreach, but worth thinking).

Attachments for the final doc: screenshots of prom graphs, node-exporter CSV dump, kube-proxy logs aggregated (saved to S3:/incidents/2024-11-03-iptables-dns), and the rollback PR for kube-proxy flags (#198).

Status: Draft -> will convert to final incident review after follow-up actions closed and CI scheduling root cause confirmed.

-- end of scratchpad --
